subject: principles-of-accounts
title: Double Entry: One Purchase, Two Accounts

slides.heading: Double Entry: One Purchase, Two Accounts
bullets: How one cash purchase of equipment changes two accounts at once: cash falls by $4,000, equipment rises by $4,000, and the accounting equation stays balanced
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we follow one purchase through both accounts it changes, from the opening balanced position to the re-checked balanced position.

slides.heading: What we will learn
bullets: Describe double entry in order: opening balance, the purchase, both accounts changing by the same $4,000, the equation re-checked
Explain why total assets stay at $10,000 when cash is swapped for equipment of equal value
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud and tell the class: by the end you will be able to trace both sides of one transaction and prove the equation still balances.

slides.heading: Cash leaves the till - has the business lost value?
bullets: The business starts with $10,000 cash and no equipment
It pays $4,000 cash for equipment, so what does it hold now?
slides.notes: Ask the class: cash has gone out, so is there less value in the business than before? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the cash was swapped, not lost.

slides.heading: Every transaction is recorded twice
bullets: Double entry means each transaction is recorded in the two accounts it changes
Paying cash for equipment cuts the cash account and raises the equipment account by the same amount
Assets = Capital + Liabilities must balance before and after every transaction
slides.notes: Stress the deciding idea: one purchase, two accounts, same amount on both sides of the change - that is what keeps the equation balanced.

slides.heading: Opening position: the equation balances
bullets: The business opens with $10,000 cash, provided by the owner as capital, and owes nothing
Assets of $10,000 equal capital of $10,000 plus liabilities of $0
slides.notes: Play scene 1 and point to the three boxes: cash $10,000, capital $10,000, liabilities $0 - the equation balances at the start.

slides.heading: The purchase: cash flows out, equipment arrives
bullets: The business pays $4,000 cash for equipment
Cash flows out at the same moment as the equipment arrives
slides.notes: Play scene 2 and watch both movements together: the payment and the arrival are one transaction, not two separate events.

slides.heading: Both accounts change by the same $4,000
bullets: The cash account falls by $4,000, from $10,000 to $6,000
The equipment account rises by $4,000, from $0 to $4,000
slides.notes: Play scene 3 slowly: name the two changes together - down $4,000 in cash, up $4,000 in equipment, so the total has not moved.

slides.heading: Re-checked: the equation still balances
bullets: Total assets are $6,000 cash plus $4,000 equipment, still $10,000
Assets = Capital + Liabilities still balances, with capital $10,000 and liabilities $0
slides.notes: Play scene 4 and re-add the assets aloud: $6,000 plus $4,000 is $10,000, exactly the opening total.

slides.heading: Worked example: tracing the $4,000 purchase
bullets: Start with cash $10,000, pay $4,000 for equipment, and record the fall in cash and the rise in equipment at the same moment
Cash $6,000 plus equipment $4,000 gives total assets of $10,000, so the equation still balances
slides.notes: Work it slowly: Step 1, opening cash $10,000. Step 2, pay $4,000 cash. Step 3, cash falls to $6,000 and equipment rises to $4,000. Step 4, total assets stay at $10,000 and the equation balances.

slides.heading: Your turn: record both sides
bullets: In pairs: state both accounts changed by the $4,000 purchase, the direction of each change, and the new total assets
Then swap and check: did your partner record both changes, instead of only the cash going out?
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes. Listen for two-account reasoning, then take two pairs answers: cash down $4,000, equipment up $4,000, total assets unchanged at $10,000.

slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
bullets: Your exit ticket asks you to correct a student who says paying cash for equipment leaves the business with fewer assets
Name both accounts, both $4,000 changes, and the unchanged $10,000 total to earn full credit
slides.notes: Point to the exit ticket and remind the class: the strongest answers follow both accounts - cash down, equipment up, total unchanged.
